label: Aber Gateway
info:
# __GATEWAY_NAME__

This flow is a STARTING POINT, not a finished integration. It does three things:

1. publishes a gateway heartbeat every 30s, which is what makes this gateway show ONLINE
2. reports this appliance's own health on that heartbeat -- uptime, load, free memory, free disk,
   the bundle version, the hash of the flow it last deployed, and when the broker CA expires
3. publishes device readings BY EXCEPTION: what moved, plus a refresh every 120s -- demonstrated by
   one example device, which also shows zero-touch onboarding

## What this appliance reports about itself

`node_exporter` runs beside Node-RED (see `docker-compose.yml`) and is **not** published: the
platform does not scrape it, because this appliance's connection is outbound only and an inbound
path per gateway is exactly what that design avoids. The **poll host metrics** branch reads it over
the local network every 60s and caches three series; the heartbeat publishes whatever is cached.

**A collector that is down costs three metrics and never the heartbeat.** The poll is on its own
timer for that reason -- a gateway that stopped beating because a disk-usage collector was slow
would be reported STALE and then OFFLINE, which is a far worse failure than the one it reports on.
Readings older than five minutes are dropped rather than republished, so the figure on the
dashboard is always one this appliance actually took.

The **flow hash** is read from `/data/gitops/deployed.json`, which `flow-sync` writes after every
deploy and `bootstrap` writes at enrolment. The platform holds the hash of `flows.json` at the head
of `main`, so the dashboard can say whether this appliance has deployed what was approved. An edit
made in this editor is not reflected in it; the next approved deploy overwrites such an edit.

`Cert_Expires_At` is the one worth understanding. The broker's CA is copied by hand into every
appliance's trust store, so re-minting it takes a whole fleet offline at once with no signal but
absence. Reporting the date THIS appliance holds turns that into a month's warning. It is read once
at enrolment, from the CA that was installed -- replace that file by hand and the reported date
will not follow it.

## Adding your own device

Send readings to **publish by exception** as `msg.payload = { device: "<id>", metrics: { <name>:
<value> } }`, from your own flow through a link-out to **device readings**. The first reading
births the device, and it appears in the dashboard's **quarantine queue**: its data is dropped until
an operator approves it. That is the intended path; you do not pre-register anything. The **example
reading** node does exactly this for a device called `press-01`.

## This appliance publishes what changed, not everything on a timer

A reading is published when it moves: any change for a boolean or a string, and for a number any
change unless you set a deadband for it at the top of **publish by exception**. Every 120s each
device's metrics are republished at their last values. That refresh is the proof of life: it tells a
steady machine from a dead sensor, and it keeps the device ONLINE on the platform, which marks one
OFFLINE after 300s of silence. Publishing a static value every few seconds writes the same row
into the historian thousands of times a day; this does not.

## When the platform cannot be reached

Everything this flow publishes passes through **store and forward**, which also holds the
Sparkplug session. With a primary host named at enrolment it births only once that host says on
`spBv1.0/STATE/<id>` that it is online. While no reading can be delivered -- the broker is
unreachable, or the node is waiting for the host -- device readings are written to `/data/buffer`
and replayed with `is_historical` set after the next birth. Heartbeats and births are not buffered:
they say what is true now. After each outage the heartbeat reports when it started and ended and
how many readings were buffered and dropped. The limits are at the top of the node.

## What you may NOT publish

The broker confines this gateway to `spBv1.0/+/+/__SPARKPLUG_ID__/#`. A message published under
any other edge node is dropped by the broker, silently, by design -- it is what stops one gateway
forging another's telemetry.

name: READ ME — this appliance publishes as __SPARKPLUG_ID__ and nothing else
info:
The broker pins the topic's edge-node segment to this gateway's own username
(a role generated for it at the broker). Publishing under a different edge node
is not an error you will see -- the broker drops the message and tells the client nothing.

The credential is in `flows_cred.json`, encrypted. It is not recoverable from this appliance and
not re-issuable except by generating a new bundle in the dashboard.

This appliance publishes what changed, not everything on a timer. The heartbeat is the gateway's
proof of life; the refresh every 120s is each device's.

name: build node-level message
example reading
DEVICE READINGS — published by exception, not on a timer
info: Send `{ device, metrics }` to **publish by exception**: from the example here, or from your own flows through the **device readings** link. It births each device, then publishes only the metrics that moved. The heartbeat above is the gateway's proof of life; the refresh below is each device's, republishing every metric at its last value.

name: publish by exception
STORE AND FORWARD — readings wait on disk while the platform cannot be reached
info:
Everything this appliance publishes passes through **store and forward**, and it holds the Sparkplug session: it connects the broker node itself, with an NDEATH carrying a fresh bdSeq as the Last Will and as the message sent before a deliberate disconnect.

With a primary host named in `/data/gateway.env` (`GATEWAY_PRIMARY_HOST_ID`, from enrolment), it births only once that host's `spBv1.0/STATE/<id>` says it is online, and when the host goes offline it disconnects and connects again, as Sparkplug 3.0.0 requires. While no reading can be delivered, readings are appended to `/data/buffer`; after the next birth they are replayed in timestamp order with `is_historical` set, so the platform files each at the time it was read.

The buffer is bounded (`MAX_BYTES`, 256 MiB, and `MAX_AGE_DAYS`, 7): when it is full the oldest readings are dropped and counted. After every outage the heartbeat reports the window and the readings buffered and dropped, so the platform states what an outage cost even when nothing was buffered. Set `BUFFER_ENABLED` to false to keep nothing.

The wire is Sparkplug B protobuf, encoded in this node; the rest of the flow builds plain objects.

name: on start — the session starts again
store and forward
a buffer file that is not there
REBIRTH REQUESTS — answered with a birth of the node or the device
info: The platform asks for a rebirth when this node's seq jumps, because a message was lost. An NCMD re-births the node and every device at its last values; a DCMD re-births one device. Nothing else sent here is acted on.

name: answer a rebirth request
HOST METRICS — polled locally, never scraped from the centre
info:
node_exporter runs beside Node-RED on this appliance (see docker-compose.yml) and is NOT published.

The platform's Prometheus does not scrape it, and that is deliberate: this appliance's connection is
outbound only, gateways enrol dynamically so a static scrape config cannot know them, and an inbound
path per gateway is the thing an outbound-only design exists to avoid.

So the flow polls it over the local compose network and publishes three series on the MQTT connection
it already holds. The poll is on its own timer and writes to a cache; the heartbeat reads that cache.
A node_exporter that is down costs three metrics and never the heartbeat.

name: select and cache
DEPLOYED FLOW — what flow-sync last wrote, reported on the heartbeat
info:
flow-sync.mjs writes /data/gitops/deployed.json after every deploy (the commit, the branch, the SHA-256
of the flow it wrote), and bootstrap.mjs writes the same record for the enrolment flow. This branch reads
it every 60s into the flow cache, and the heartbeat reports the hash from there as `Flow_Hash`.

The platform records the SHA-256 of flows.json at the head of main on every push, so the two hashes
side by side say whether this appliance has deployed what was approved. A reload does not re-source
gateway.env, which is why this is a file and not an environment variable.

Same rule as the host-metrics branch: this writes to a cache and the heartbeat reads it. An unreadable
file costs one metric and never the heartbeat.

name: parse and cache
BROKER ROOT — what this appliance trusts, reported on the heartbeat
info:
bootstrap.mjs writes /data/certs/ca.json for the root enrolment installed, and
aber-gateway-converge rewrites it whenever the platform publishes a bundle this appliance did
not already hold. This branch reads it every 60s into the flow cache, and the heartbeat reports
`not_after_ms` from there as `Cert_Expires_At`.

A FILE AND NOT AN ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE. The root changes between two container starts -- the
converge script installs a new bundle and restarts this container -- and a reload does not
re-source gateway.env, so a value put there would be the enrolment root’s date forever.

Same rule as the other two collector branches: this writes to a cache and the heartbeat reads
it. An unreadable file costs one metric and never the heartbeat.
